evidence: Sen. Ep. 106.12: nōn vītae sed scholae discimus
terms.comment: The plain “but”, which sets the second thing against the first; after a negative, “not … but” is nōn … sed. Many English “buts” need no word in Latin, where two clauses side by side make the contrast; and a light “but” that only moves on is autem (see however). Don’t open sentence after sentence with sed.

evidence: Verg. G. 4.6: in tenuī labor; at tenuis nōn glōria
terms.comment: A sharper “but”: an objection in speech (“but, you’ll say …”), a protest (At!), or a sudden turn to another person or scene.

evidence: Phaedr. 3 prol. 49–50: neque enim notāre singulōs mēns est mihi, vērum ipsam vītam et mōrēs hominum ostendere
terms.comment: After a negative, the same as sed; in nōn modo … vērum etiam, not only … but also.

phrases.english: but you are dawdling, and the day is going

phrases.english: but memory fades. — I dare say, if you don’t exercise it

phrases.latin: in tenuī labor; at tenuis nōn glōria
phrases.english: the work is on a small thing, but the glory is not small
